h1:
A Local Ranong Breakfast
Dim Sum, Kopi, Khanom Jeen, Markets
intro: If you sleep in when you visit Ranong, you miss half of what makes this town good, because breakfast is when Ranong actually comes alive. Locals get up to sip kopi, order dim sum by the basket, then walk into the municipal market for crab-curry khanom jeen and Burmese-style noodles. This is a border town where Thais, Hokkien Chinese, and Burmese have lived side by side for generations, and the morning plates here mix together in a way you won't find anywhere else.

blocks.html: Ranong is a town you have to eat in the morning. Honestly, a lot of the best places only open from early morning to noon and then close, so if you get up in the afternoon you'll just find shuttered shops. The breakfast culture here has three roots: dim sum and kopi from the Hokkien Chinese who came to mine tin more than a hundred years ago, southern-style khanom jeen with curry sauce, and Burmese breakfasts from the workers and Myanmar community who have been part of this town for a long time. We've picked out what to eat when you get up early in Ranong, which shops, and which neighborhoods.

blocks.text: Morning dim sum in Ranong — start the day like a local

blocks.html: Dim sum is the main breakfast for people in Ranong — not a fancy treat but an everyday meal. Most shops keep a steamer puffing away out front, and you order small baskets for 20–25 THB each, eaten with kopi or hot tea. Many places also have pork-blood soup, braised chicken feet in red sauce, and clay-pot rice with salted olive to order on the side. These are the shops Ranong locals and reviewers mention most often.

items.name: Ranong Ocha Dim Sum
items.blurb: The most talked-about dim sum shop in town. Freshly steamed dim sum at 25 THB a basket with dozens of choices. The dishes people order again and again are the clay-pot rice with salted olive, eggs in a hot pan, bak kut teh, and braised chicken feet in red sauce. It ranks near the top of all restaurants in the province on review sites. Weekends get packed, so go before 9 a.m.
items.meta: Soi Chaloem Phrakiat, Khao Niwet · Breakfast · 25 THB/basket

items.name: Pee Ton Ranong Breakfast
items.blurb: A full-on breakfast with everything on the plate: dim sum, red barbecue pork, crispy pork, pork-blood soup — one order gets you both steamed dishes and rice plates. Good for when you're really hungry in the morning. Open until noon, so no need to rush like at the other shops.

items.name: Tha Mueang Dim Sum
items.blurb: An early-morning dim sum shop in Soi Buppha Chon, open at 6 a.m. and closing early around 10. This is where the genuine early risers sit, with hot dim sum coming out of the steamer non-stop and the feel of an old-neighborhood spot.

items.name: Sueng Kopi Dim Sum
items.blurb: A shop that pairs kopi and dim sum in one place. Order a hot cup of old-school coffee and keep nibbling dim sum at your own pace — an easy breakfast where you get the old-coffee atmosphere and the steamed dishes all under one roof.
items.meta: In town · Breakfast · Kopi 20–30 THB · Dim sum 25 THB

blocks.title: How to order dim sum
blocks.html: Most dim sum shops charge by the number of baskets stacked on your table, so ordering a little at a time and topping up makes it easier to keep an eye on your budget. And don't forget to order a kopi or hot tea alongside — you almost never see a Ranong local eat dim sum on its own.

blocks.text: Kopi — the old-school coffee Ranong can't do without

blocks.html: Kopi is Hokkien-style traditional coffee, brewed through a cloth filter, with dark-roasted beans blended with butter — heavy, sweet, and rich, poured over with condensed milk and drunk hot in the morning. It's the perfect partner to dim sum and toast with sangkhaya custard. Kopi shops in Ranong are still where the older folks come to chat every morning, so if you want to see the real rhythm of this town, go sit down for a cup.

items: Hot kopi — old-school coffee with condensed milk, dark, sweet, and rich, around 20–30 THB a cup. Order it with custard toast or a soft-boiled egg.
Hot tea (tiam) — tea with condensed milk, made the same way as kopi, for people who don't drink coffee. Fragrant and just sweet enough.
Oliang — for a hot morning: iced black coffee, easy on the wallet, found at just about every old-coffee shop.
Custard toast + soft-boiled egg — the classic kopi pairing. Crispy toast spread with pandan custard, eaten with a soft-boiled egg dressed in soy sauce and white pepper — a classic morning set.

blocks.title: Where to find kopi shops
blocks.html: Walk around Ruangrat Road, the old Sino-Portuguese quarter in the center of town, and you'll find plenty of traditional coffee shops and dim sum spots serving kopi. Stroll past the old buildings while you sip — it makes for a well-rounded Ranong morning.

blocks.text: Ranong khanom jeen — crab curry is the star

blocks.html: Khanom jeen is a southern-style breakfast, and Ranong does it really well. What sets it apart is the crab curry sauce — a thick sauce made with real crab meat, naturally sweet from the crab itself, eaten with a big pile of fresh raw vegetables. These are the khanom jeen shops Ranong locals stand behind.

items.name: Je Anne Crab-Curry Khanom Jeen
items.blurb: A crab-curry khanom jeen shop that many say was the first in Ranong. It's inside the fresh market, with several sauces to choose from — crab curry, green curry, and tai pla curry — but the one to order is the crab curry at 25 THB a plate: real crab meat, rich sauce.
items.meta: Inside Ranong fresh market · Breakfast · 25 THB/plate

items.name: Je Kob Khanom Jeen
items.blurb: A tucked-away shop in front of Wat Wari Banphot (Wat Bang Non), known for a huge buffet of fresh raw vegetables and several rich curry sauces to choose from. Veggie lovers will especially like it. Open from morning into early afternoon.
items.meta: By Wat Bang Non · 7:30–13:00 · from 45 THB

items.name: Ji Nguan Khanom Jeen
items.blurb: An old khanom jeen shop in town that locals have eaten at for years. The sauce is a mellow southern style — nothing flashy, but steady and reliable on every plate. Good for anyone who likes traditional khanom jeen.
items.meta: In Ranong town · Breakfast · from 40 THB

blocks.text: The municipal market — a Burmese breakfast you won't find elsewhere

blocks.html: This is what makes a Ranong breakfast different from other towns. Ranong is a border town with a real Myanmar community, so the municipal market has Burmese-style breakfasts sold right alongside Thai food. The standout is Dawei-style khanom jeen, or mohinga — Burmese noodles in a clear-to-yellow herbal fish soup, with a flavor clearly different from southern curry. Eat it with Burmese-style fritters that look like a cross between Chinese doughnuts and samosas. To get this you have to walk into the market yourself — you won't find it at regular restaurants.

items.name: Dawei khanom jeen / mohinga
items.blurb: Burmese noodles in a clear herbal fish soup, milder than southern curry but with a clear spice aroma. Burmese people eat it as an everyday breakfast — try a plate to understand this town.

items.name: Burmese fritters + hot tea
items.blurb: Fried dough that looks like a mix of Chinese doughnuts and samosas, eaten with Burmese-style milk tea. Find it at the tea shops in the Burmese market area on Phoem Phon Road.

blocks.title: Make the most of the morning market
blocks.html: The municipal market is busiest from early morning through mid-morning, so go before 8 a.m. to get the freshest food while all the stalls are still going. Bring cash, since most stalls in the market only take cash. Keep an open mind and you'll come across food you've never seen anywhere else.

blocks.text: How to eat a full Ranong breakfast in one morning

blocks.html: If you only have one morning but want to hit all three traditions, try a graze-as-you-go plan like this. You'll get dim sum, kopi, khanom jeen, and Burmese food all in a single morning.

blocks.label: One morning
blocks.title: Eating across three cultures at breakfast

items.activity: Start at an early dim sum shop. Order 3–4 baskets of dim sum with a hot kopi.
items.note: Tha Mueang Dim Sum or Pee Ton open earliest. Don't over-order — save room.

items.activity: Walk into the municipal market and find a plate of Burmese Dawei khanom jeen or mohinga.
items.note: Grab some Burmese fritters to snack on as you go.

items.activity: Finish with Je Anne's crab-curry khanom jeen in the fresh market, eaten with a big pile of raw vegetables.
items.note: Crab curry at 25 THB a plate is the highlight of this morning.

items.activity: Walk it off along Ruangrat Road, look at the old Sino-Portuguese buildings, and stop at a kopi shop for a final coffee.
items.note: Custard toast with a soft-boiled egg makes a good sweet ending to the meal.

items: The best shops close early — many dim sum and khanom jeen places only sell from morning to noon or early afternoon, so sleeping in usually means missing out. If you have your heart set on a specific shop, check the hours first.
Bring cash — most market stalls and old-coffee shops take cash, so don't count on transfers or cards working everywhere.
Weekends get crowded — popular spots like Ranong Ocha have long lines on weekends. Going before 9 a.m. is easier.
Keep an open mind about the flavors — Dawei khanom jeen and Burmese mohinga don't taste like southern curry. Try them with an open mind: some people love them, some shrug, but it's worth a go.

faq.q: What breakfasts should you try in Ranong?
faq.a: Three things you shouldn't miss: dim sum with kopi in the Hokkien Chinese style, southern crab-curry khanom jeen, and Burmese Dawei khanom jeen or mohinga in the municipal market. Eat all three and you understand this border town on a plate.

faq.q: Where's the best dim sum in Ranong?
faq.a: The most talked-about shop is Ranong Ocha Dim Sum on Soi Chaloem Phrakiat, with dim sum at 25 THB a basket and dozens of choices. If you want a place that opens very early, try Tha Mueang Dim Sum in Soi Buppha Chon, or Pee Ton, which stays open until noon.

faq.q: Where can you eat crab-curry khanom jeen in Ranong?
faq.a: Je Anne's crab-curry khanom jeen inside the Ranong fresh market — many say it was the first in the province — has crab curry at 25 THB a plate with real crab meat. Another favorite is Je Kob in front of Wat Bang Non, known for its big buffet of raw vegetables.

faq.q: What time do Ranong breakfast shops open?
faq.a: Most open early, around 6 a.m. until noon or early afternoon. Some dim sum shops close early, around 10 a.m., while khanom jeen usually sells until about 1 p.m. Going before 9 a.m. gets you the full spread without a long wait.

faq.q: Where can you find a Burmese breakfast in Ranong?
faq.a: In the municipal market and the Burmese market area along Phoem Phon Road you'll find Dawei khanom jeen or mohinga, plus Burmese fritters that look like a cross between Chinese doughnuts and samosas, eaten with hot milk tea — a breakfast you can't get in other towns.
